2.text: in its turn, on a tray (Fig. 102, a³). Sometimes this bowl and tray are

3.text: made of one piece (Fig. 102, a²). Another

4.text: tray serves as a support for the whole.

5.text: All these vessels serve to catch the drip-

6.text: pings of oil. The material used for lighting

7.text: is either blubber, or, in all inland regions,

8.text: the tallow tried out of the reindeer-bones,

9.text: which have been crushed with a stone ham-

10.text: mer. The latter material is the better,

11.text: because reindeer-tallow is very hard and

12.text: contains a large proportion of stearine. It

13.text: burns with a soft bright light, without smoke

14.text: or odor. The wick is made of sphagnum

15.text: thoroughly dried and spread in a thin nar-

16.text: row layer across the front edge of the lamp.

17.text: To burn properly it requires continual trim-

18.text: ming, which is done with a slender chip of

19.text: wood. Instead of sphagnum, rotten wood

20.text: or thin half-burnt shavings may be used.

21.text: The lamp inside has a bridge, flat and in-

22.text: clined backwards. Its edges do not reach

23.text: the sides of the lamp, and the middle has a deep cleft almost to the level

24.text: of the bottom. The fuel, blubber, or tallow is placed behind the bridge, and

25.text: the lamp is set in its wooden bowl somewhat obliquely. The slant causes

26.text: the oil oozing from the blubber, or the melting tallow, to flow down to the

27.text: wick along the walls of the lamp or through the cleft in the dividing ridge.

28.text: Pounded blubber is sometimes used in the lamp to make the extraction of

29.text: the oil easier. Oftentimes the lamp is simply filled with oil, and placed on

30.text: the tray in a horizontal position, though it is then much more apt to

31.text: smoke. The seal-oil lamp also gives off a strong unpleasant smell, offensive

33.text: The ordinary lamp of the people, both Maritime Chukchee and Eskimo

34.text: (Fig. 103, a), is larger than that used by the Reindeer people. It has an

35.text: oval, almost rectangular shape, and is made of clay. The bridge is vertical.

36.text: For cooking, still larger lamps, with two bridges (Fig. 103, b) and moss

37.text: wicks arranged on both sides of the lamp, are used. The bridges are often

38.text: divided in the middle. The lamp is placed horizontally on a large wooden

39.text: dish, and the kettle suspended over it from a peg. Round lamps of clay

40.text: and sandstone are also used, and sometimes are put in a large round kettle-

41.text: shaped vessel of clay, with one side cut out in a half-circle (Fig. 104, a) to

42.text: give a better support to the oblique position of the lamp.¹
